title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography
summary: Steganography hides data inside another file so the carrier still looks and usually still works like an ordinary image, audio clip, video, or text document. Unlike encryption, which makes content unreadable but obvious, steganography aims to hide that anything is concealed at all, and the two are often combined so the embedded payload is also encrypted. The hidden bytes may sit in unused colour values, after the logical end of a media file, or in metadata and whitespace, and a small extractor recovers them at the other end. Documented cases include malware that encrypted collected data into an image before sending it to a command server, and scripts that stored executable instructions inside a picture. Defenders look for size or entropy that does not match the visible content, trailing data after an image end marker, and processes that read a media file and immediately open a network connection.

beginner.definition: Steganography means hiding a secret message inside something ordinary, such as a photo. The photo still looks normal when you open it. Only someone who knows the trick can pull the hidden message out. This is different from locking a message in a safe.
beginner.whyItMatters: Encrypted files look suspicious, but a normal holiday photo does not. Security tools often allow pictures and music to pass without close inspection. An attacker can hide stolen data or hidden commands inside them. Because people share these files all the time, hidden content can travel far.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a carrier file, such as a picture or a sound clip.
They change tiny details that people cannot see or hear, and store data there.
They may also add extra data after the end of the file, where viewers stop reading.
The carrier is then sent or shared like any other ordinary media file.
At the other end, a small tool reads the hidden bytes and rebuilds the message.
The hidden data is often encrypted as well, so even discovery does not reveal it.
beginner.example: Think of a letter where the first letter of each sentence spells a secret word. The letter reads normally, and the postman sees nothing odd. Only a reader who knows the rule finds the hidden message. Steganography hides data in a file in the same way.
takeaways: Steganography hides that a message exists, unlike encryption which hides only its meaning.
Mismatched file size, odd trailing data, and strange read patterns are useful clues.
Combine media file inspection with network behaviour when you investigate.

objectives: Explain what steganography is and how it differs from encryption.
Describe common carrier files and the places where hidden data is stored.
Identify file level clues that suggest a carrier holds hidden content.
Explain how hidden content relates to command and control or exfiltration.
Describe why ordinary media traffic makes this technique hard to spot.
